readerTitle: Where word of mouth is really paid for
caseNote: 가상 사례 (지역 화물 배송 회사, 치과 예약 앱) + 실제 연구 (Berger & Schwartz 2011, Trusov 외 2009) · 모든 사업 수치는 설명용
insight: 입소문은 마케팅 예산이 아니라 운영 예산에서 만들어진다. 고객 경험을 줄이는 비용 절감은 보이지 않는 획득 비용을 올린다.
misconception: 추천으로 온 고객은 공짜다. 입소문은 운이거나 제품이 좋으면 저절로 생긴다.

sources.text: Berger, J., & Schwartz, E. M. (2011). What Drives Immediate and Ongoing Word of Mouth? Journal of Marketing Research, 48(5), 869–880.
Trusov, M., Bucklin, R. E., & Pauwels, K. (2009). Effects of Word-of-Mouth Versus Traditional Marketing: Findings from an Internet Social Networking Site. Journal of Marketing, 73(5), 90–102.
배송 회사와 치과 예약 앱의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Berger & Schwartz(2011)의 핵심 결론(흥미로운 제품은 즉각적 입소문은 더 받지만 지속적 입소문은 더 받지 않으며, 주변 환경에서 자주 떠올려지는(cued) 제품이 지속적 입소문을 더 받는다)을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
Trusov 외(2009): 소셜 네트워킹 사이트에서 입소문 추천이 마케팅 이벤트·언론 보도보다 신규 가입에 더 오래 지속되는 효과를 보였다는 결론을 원문으로 확인하세요. 구체적 탄력성 수치는 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
'추천 1/3 감소'는 설명을 위한 가정입니다. 카드 본문에 'Suppose'로 가정임을 밝혔습니다.

cards.title: Where word of mouth is really paid for
body: A regional delivery company won 100 new business customers last year. Forty came from trade ads that cost $40,000. The other 60 said a colleague recommended it.
On the marketing report, those 60 customers cost nothing. That zero is about to cause an expensive mistake.

image.label: Delivery van with speech bubbles passing between businesses
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 배송 트럭이 거리를 지나가고, 주변 가게와 창고 사이로 말풍선이 오감. 한쪽에 "Ads: 40", 말풍선 쪽에 "Recommended: 60" 라벨. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Cut the dispatcher who calls ahead?
body: Your operations manager wants to cut one role: the dispatcher who phones customers before a shipment runs late and offers a fix. It saves $35,000 a year.
Deliveries won't get slower. Customers just won't hear about problems first. What do you do?

options.text: Cut it. Delivery speed stays the same, so marketing isn't affected
options.feedback: You bank $35,000 for sure, but you may be cutting the reason 60 customers got recommended. That cost won't show up in operations at all.

options.text: First ask recommended customers what they told their colleagues
options.feedback: It delays the saving, but you learn whether the calls are part of the story people repeat. That tells you what the role really earns.

options.text: Cut it, and move part of the saving into ads
options.feedback: Ads can replace some lost customers, at about $1,000 each. But you'd be paying cash for what the dispatcher earned you through talk.

cards.title: Suppose recommendations drop by a third.
body: The saving turns into a **$25,000 loss** in the first year. And that ignores current customers who leave after an unwarned late delivery.
cards.softwareNote: Your free channel is often your support team or your reliability. Cutting either can raise acquisition cost without touching the marketing budget.

cards.title: Word of mouth
body: **Word of mouth** is customers telling other people about you, on their own and unpaid.

It looks free because no invoice arrives. But it is paid for, just somewhere else: in the experience. Here, the phone call before a late delivery was the story customers retold: *"They warned me before I even knew."*
Cut the experience, and you quietly cut the channel.

image.label: Marketing budget sheet next to a warehouse dispatch desk
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 "Marketing budget" 문서, 오른쪽은 전화기를 든 배차 담당자 책상. 오른쪽에서 말풍선이 나와 왼쪽 문서의 "Recommended customers" 칸으로 이어지는 화살표.

cards.title: Talk lasts, and reminders keep it going.
body: A 2009 study of a social networking site by Trusov, Bucklin and Pauwels found that sign-ups from word-of-mouth referrals kept coming longer than those from marketing events or press coverage.

Jonah Berger and Eric Schwartz (2011) found that *interesting* products got more talk at first, but not more over time. Products people were reminded of often, by everyday cues, kept getting talked about.

cards.title: People talk when they have something to say.
body: Three things tend to give customers a reason to mention you:
list: **A story:** a problem solved, a surprise, a rescue
**A reminder:** a moment that brings you to mind, like a delivery or a weekly report
**An easy line:** one sentence they can repeat without effort
cards.callout: Ask of any change: does it add a story, or remove one?

cards.title: Word of mouth is slow and hard to count.
body: "How did you hear about us?" is a rough measure. People forget, and many hear from a colleague *and* see an ad.
It also cuts both ways. A bad experience is a story too, and it can travel among the same people.
And you can't order it. If the experience is merely fine, asking for recommendations gets little. Paying people to talk is a different tool, with its own costs.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app for dental clinics.
body: Clinic managers mention your appointment app to each other at regional meetups. You also hear complaints: text reminders sometimes fail, and patients miss visits.
You have budget for one project this quarter. Which grows word of mouth most?

options.text: Fix the reminder bug, and add a monthly "missed visits saved" report
options.feedback: You remove a bad story and give managers a good one with a number attached. It's slower than ads but builds talk that keeps going.

options.text: Offer managers $100 for every clinic they refer
options.feedback: It may bring sign-ups, but paid talk is a different tool. The complaint people repeat at meetups stays unfixed.

options.text: Spend the budget on ads in dental trade magazines
options.feedback: Ads buy attention fast. But new clinics will meet the same failing reminders and may say so at the next meetup.

cards.title: Word of mouth is earned in operations, not bought in marketing.
body: Before cutting a cost, ask whether it's part of the story customers tell about you.
**Try it today:** ask three customers who were recommended to you what their friend actually said. Write down the exact words.
